Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: No specific evidence found on rural police stations' recording methods. Recent urban innovations like unmanned smart police stations (2026) and Digital Ethiopia 2030 focus on Addis Ababa pilots with digital kiosks for reporting, eliminating paperwork there. Courts have e-filing (2025). However, UNODC reports emphasize training and capacity building without digital case systems; HR reports detail poor conditions in police stations but no digital mentions. Rural areas likely retain traditional paper-based practices (occurrence books, manual files) as digitisation is urban/pilot-focused. Score 1 as broad evidence indicates paper dominance outside pilots.

revision_notes: The state.gov human rights report URL returned a technical/access error on fetch and could not be independently verified; the ena.et and UNODC evaluation report URLs were not re-fetched but remain consistent with corroborating evidence found elsewhere. Fresh search confirms rural/traditional police stations remain paper-based: BBC (March 2026) reports the AI-driven 'smart police station' remains a single pilot in Addis Ababa's Bole district, with traditional stations - including rural ones - continuing to rely on in-person, paper-based reporting; a Federal Police-AI Institute smart station agreement (July 2025) and a Ministry of Justice Criminal Record Information Management System (CRIMS) project (2026) are both still at pilot/development stage and Addis Ababa-focused. Score 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed for rural stations as of 2026.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Ethiopia continue to rely on entirely paper-based record keeping. Digitalisation initiatives such as the AI Institute-Federal Police smart station pilot in Addis Ababa's Bole district, launched in February 2026, and the Criminal Record Information Management System (CRIMS) project remain confined to the capital and are still at pilot or early development stage. Traditional police stations, which include all rural facilities, continue in-person, paper-based reporting and record keeping, with no evidence of digital data capture at the point of service.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices (kebeles, 92% of operational sites) in Ethiopia rely entirely on paper-based manual registration using bound booklets with carbon copies; original stays local, copies transmitted upward.UNECA CRVS Ethiopia Snapshot Digitalisation limited to urban pilots (100 kebeles in Addis Ababa computerized; tablet ME-CRVS in 1,300 kebeles, fragmented home-grown/open-source systems in regions like Oromia/Amhara).Strengthening CRVS Presentation No evidence of routine point-of-service digital use in most rural facilities; paper default despite national plans for standardization.UNECA Digitalisation Assessment Key barriers: inadequate ICT infrastructure, electricity/network interruptions, rugged terrain limiting access (up to 8hr walks), transport/support lacks, low awareness/demand. National policy (Digital Ethiopia 2030, CRVS Strategy 2022-26, 2025 Proclamation) aims full digital linkage to NID/Fayda ID, but rural reality lags far behind urban pilots due to infrastructure gaps, conflicts reducing kebele ops from 90% to 70%.

revision_notes: The UNECA snapshot PDF timed out on re-fetch (CRAWL_LIVECRAWL_TIMEOUT) but its findings (paper booklets with carbon copies, only around 100 kebeles in Addis Ababa computerised) were corroborated via search excerpt and by fresher 2025 sources. Updated search confirms rural kebele registration remains predominantly paper-based: a July 2025 CRVS presentation records a tablet-based ME-CRVS system piloted in only around 1,300 of roughly 19,200 kebeles (under 7%), with kebele operational coverage at 70% (down from 90% due to conflict); a November 2025 Capital Newspaper report finds the mobile registration platform accounts for only around 24% of total registrations nationally, concentrated where connectivity is better; a December 2025 Fana Media report confirms that work is 'currently underway to fundamentally overhaul the existing paper-based registration system'. Score 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed as the reality for the great majority of rural kebeles as of 2025.
revised_comments: Civil registration at kebele (rural registry office) level in Ethiopia remains predominantly paper-based. Registration of vital events is recorded manually in bound booklets with carbon copies, with one copy retained locally and further copies passed up through woreda, regional and federal levels. A tablet-based mobile civil registration platform has been piloted in around 1,300 of the country's roughly 19,200 kebeles, and computerised registration exists in around 100 kebeles in Addis Ababa, but these remain isolated pilots rather than the norm. Nationally, the mobile platform accounts for only around a quarter of total registrations, concentrated in areas with better connectivity and power supply; unstable infrastructure keeps the electronic system largely symbolic across most rural areas. A comprehensive overhaul to replace the paper-based system with an integrated digital platform is under way as part of the Digital Ethiopia 2030 strategy, but rural implementation lags substantially behind urban areas.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Ethiopia predominantly use paper-based methods for recording administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes. Schools complete lengthy annual EMIS census questionnaires (25 pages) by hand, using paper registers that are often poorly maintained or stored insecurely. Data is physically transported to woreda/REB levels for manual Excel entry; no digital tools at point-of-service. Attendance tracked in registers (not centrally digitized), learning outcomes via national exams aggregated later.UNESCO ECW EMIS Case Study%20and%20Data%20for%20Increased%20Resilience%20to%20Crisis_%20country%20case%20study_%20Ethopia.pdf) Only 76-83% of schools use EMIS (declining), with most rural lacking computers (40% have working ones, 28% internet); principals handle manually.RISE GEQIP Report In Oromia (rural-heavy sample), EMIS manual/paper, rated moderate but emerging on infrastructure; shortages in ICT, budget, staff.Oromia EMIS Thesis Digital pilots (SMIS, tablets) exist but isolated/not scaled to majority rural facilities. Barriers: no electricity/computers/internet in most rural schools, low skills, transport issues, no data culture. National EMIS policy ambitious, but rural reality remains paper (score 1); aggregation digitalizes upward reports only.UNESCO ECW EMIS Case Study%20and%20Data%20for%20Increased%20Resilience%20to%20Crisis_%20country%20case%20study_%20Ethopia.pdf)

revision_notes: The original EMIS case-study and RISE GEQIP-E sources were not re-fetched in full but their findings (paper registers, manual woreda-level data entry, low computer/internet access in rural schools) are corroborated by fresh 2025/26 sources. A March 2026 Ethiopia Education Report notes that EMIS 'digitalisation' was completed for 2024/25 using AI and business intelligence, but this refers to ministry-level data processing and analysis, not facility-level data capture. A DHIS2-for-Education rollout began in four regions in November 2025 (UNICEF/HISP), again operating at woreda/zonal level. A GEQIP-E-piloted digitised school data system is expected to extend to primary schools nationally only from the 2025/26 school year and has not yet reached most rural schools. Facility-level data capture in rural primary schools therefore remains paper-based; score 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed as of the 2024/25 academic year (data published October 2025).
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Ethiopia continue to record attendance, enrolment and administrative data on paper at the point of service. Annual EMIS census data is collected via lengthy paper questionnaires completed by hand and transported to woreda and Regional Education Bureau level for manual entry, and most rural schools lack functioning computers or internet access. The Ministry of Education has completed a national EMIS upgrade using artificial intelligence and business intelligence tools for downstream data analysis, and a DHIS2-based education data system has begun roll-out in four regions with UNICEF support, but these developments operate at woreda, zonal and ministry level rather than replacing paper-based data capture inside rural school facilities. A digitised school-level data system piloted under GEQIP-E is expected to extend to primary schools nationally only from the 2025/26 school year and has not yet reached the majority of rural schools.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare in Ethiopia operates through ~17,900 health posts staffed by Health Extension Workers (HEWs). The electronic Community Health Information System (eCHIS), introduced in 2018, has been scaled to approximately 8,011 health posts (~45% of total) as of 2024, with over 25 million individuals and 6 million households registered. eCHIS is a tablet-based platform covering modules for family folders, RMNCHN, disease prevention, and NCD management. However, actual utilisation remains low: only ~50% of HEWs at equipped posts actively use it, and just 24.5% offer ANC services through the platform. A 2023 maturity assessment rated ICT infrastructure at 1.67/5, citing inadequate power supply, limited connectivity, and insufficient hardware at health posts. DHIS2 covers all 30,000+ public health facilities for aggregate reporting (95%+ completeness), but data at health posts is still primarily collected on paper then entered at district level. EMR systems exist at only 58 public facilities nationally. Key barriers include unreliable electricity and internet at rural health posts, low digital literacy, heavy workloads creating dual paper-digital reporting burdens, and staff turnover. The scale of eCHIS deployment (~45% of health posts) represents meaningful digital presence at point of service, moving beyond entirely paper-based, though paper remains the predominant method.

revision_notes: The original PMC and Frontiers sources were fetched directly and confirm the prior assessment. A September 2025 national eCHIS maturity assessment (PMC) rates overall maturity as 'repeatable' (2.24/5) and ICT infrastructure at only 1.67/5, noting that only around 32% of required tablets have been supplied and that LAN internet coverage across health facilities stands at just 28%; eCHIS is implemented in over 7,500 health posts nationally (around 42% of roughly 17,900), with more than 20 million people registered. A July 2025 Frontiers study of rural East Shewa zone confirms that 7,808 of 17,903 health posts (46%) have adopted eCHIS since 2018, but only 24.5% offer ANC and 10.2% PNC through the platform, and usage even at equipped posts lags at around 50%. This confirms mixed paper and digital data capture at the majority of rural clinics; score 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) is upheld as of 2025.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare in Ethiopia operates through around 17,900 health posts staffed by Health Extension Workers. The tablet-based electronic Community Health Information System (eCHIS), rolled out since 2018, has reached around 7,500-8,000 health posts, or roughly 42-46% of the total, with more than 20 million people registered. A national maturity assessment rates ICT infrastructure at only 1.67 out of 5, noting that only around 32% of required tablets have been supplied and that internet connectivity across health facilities stands at just 28%. Even where eCHIS is deployed, utilisation remains partial: only around a quarter of equipped health posts provide antenatal care through the platform, and roughly half of Health Extension Workers at equipped posts use it actively. Paper-based recording therefore remains the predominant method at the majority of rural health posts, with meaningful but partial digital uptake at those that have been equipped.
